conditions.question: Who has to reconstruct this reasoning without the author present?
Can this step be undone, and at what cost?
Who has to be asked or told before the work goes ahead?

values.question: Is asking someone first a courtesy you may skip?
Must someone be told first, with no yes needed?
Does someone's yes have to come first?
Does a law or regulator require a yes first?

enablement.action: agree to or object to one proposed approach

guidance.claim: Canonical sections: context and scope, goals and non-goals, the actual design, alternatives considered, cross-cutting concerns. Skip the document when the solution is unambiguous.
Most large projects start with a PRD to define the problem, followed by an RFC to propose a solution.
The request-for-discussion is the same document family, inspired by the IETF's RFC series.

Do not mistake this for a Solution Design Document, an enterprise-implementation deliverable whose content belongs in the Architecture Overview. A design doc proposes one approach for reviewers to agree to or object to.
Name the problem and whose problem it is, with no solution built in.
Solution-shaped problems pre-commit the answer.
One quantified pain beats five asserted ones.

sections.name: Problem statement
sections.question: What problem should the work solve?

guidance.claim: List non-goals beside the goals. Each should be something that could reasonably be a goal and is explicitly chosen not to be; a plain negation such as 'the system should not crash' does not count.

Distinct from Success Criteria: a goal names what the work aims at; a success criterion sets the observable threshold, with a date, at which the work counts as having met it. A goal given a number and a date has become a success criterion.

Distinct from Scope (In / Out) and Trade-offs, which also set things aside. Ask what is being set aside: an aim of this work is a non-goal here; a part of the solution goes in Scope's excluded list; a promising direction for the offering as a whole goes in Trade-offs.

sections.name: Goals and non goals
sections.question: Which goals does the work pursue?

guidance.claim: Distinct from Components & Responsibilities and the other architecture elements. Ask whether a line says what the solution does and how people use it, or how it technically holds together; the second belongs there.
A Lean Canvas keeps this deliberately thin — top features only; a design document gives it a full section.
State what the solution deliberately does not do. Pairs with Scope (In / Out).

sections.name: Solution overview
sections.question: What is the intended solution, in outline?

guidance.claim: Describe and compare the options here, including the chosen option. Decision records the commitment and why it was chosen.
Standard in RFCs, decision documents and decision records. Describe the options considered, including the chosen option.
Naming the rejected options is grammatically obligatory in the Y-statement form — 'and neglected …' — not an optional courtesy to the reader.
Check that the options are feasible, diverse and comprehensive: each could really be done, none is a small variant of another, and together they cover the realistic ways to solve the problem.
Flanking a preferred course with two deliberately unattractive alternatives simulates choice rather than offering it.
Two honest alternatives beat five straw men. Absence invites re-litigation.
Each wants an owner and a resolution path. An unowned question is a risk mislabelled.

Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: an open question is something to answer before a point can be settled; an assumption is a belief the work proceeds on and checks along the way. Proceeding without the answer turns the question into an assumption.
Compare the list across drafts: it should get shorter. A list that keeps growing means the work is not yet ready to settle.
Write 'none open' only when every question raised has been answered or recorded as an assumption, so a reader can tell it apart from a list nobody has drawn up.

sections.name: Open questions
sections.question: Which questions about the work remain open?

guidance.claim: Imposed, not chosen: regulation, budget, deadline, platform, physics.

Distinct from Cross-Cutting Concerns: a constraint is an imposed limit on the work that no design choice moves — budget, deadline, platform, what the law allows; a cross-cutting concern is an obligation every part of the solution must be designed to meet — security, privacy, accessibility. One law can supply both: a limit here, a property demanded throughout there.
Distinct from Trade-offs. Mislabelling a choice as a constraint hides a decision.

sections.name: Constraints
sections.question: What imposed limits apply to the work?

guidance.claim: At minimum, say how the solution handles security, privacy and observability (how you will see what it is doing once it runs). Design docs at Google use this section to make sure these are always taken into consideration.
Regulated domains extend the list — compliance, audit, accessibility.
Exists so these get weighed while change is still cheap.

Take accessibility requirements from WCAG 2.2, whose success criteria can each be tested; normal text, for example, needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. They apply to the brand's colours and type like everything else.

sections.name: Cross cutting concerns
sections.question: Which requirements must every part of the solution meet?

guidance.claim: For an assumption, state what is being relied on and how it will be checked. For a risk, state what could happen, its significance, and the response.
Distinct from Opportunities & Threats: there an outside condition is judged for planning; here anything inside or outside that could harm the work gets a response and someone to handle it.
Before committing, imagine the work has already failed and have each person write down why. This brings out risks people hesitate to raise.
The RFC tradition records drawbacks — known, accepted costs — separately from risks, which are uncertainties.
Where an approver or regulator will review the work, date each entry and name its owner and response, so the record can be audited.

sections.name: Risks and assumptions
sections.question: What could harm the work if it happened or proved wrong?

guidance.claim: Sort the steps by whether they can be walked back. A step you can reverse is a two-way door and deserves speed; a step you cannot is a one-way door and deserves deliberation. Applying the heavy process to everything is as costly a mistake as applying the light one to the irreversible.
Name what each step forecloses, not merely what it enables. An order that closes no doors is a preference, not a sequence.
Honestly empty means every step is independently reversible in any order — in which case say so, because that is the licence to move fast.

sections.name: Sequence and foreclosure
sections.question: In what order must the work proceed?

guidance.claim: Give each stage its audience, such as a pilot group, a wider beta or everyone, and the observation that would stop or roll back the rollout before the next stage.
Distinct from Sequence & Foreclosure: rollout stages how widely the solution is introduced, with a stopping condition per stage; sequence orders the work's own steps by what each forecloses.
Enterprise implementation practice treats this as a core deliverable section. Product briefs include it only when release risk warrants.

sections.name: Rollout and phasing
sections.question: In what stages do we introduce the solution?

guidance.claim: Say what each precedent teaches the work: what to copy and what to avoid. A list of look-alikes with no lesson is not prior art.
A standard RFC section: precedent survey across other systems, organisations or communities.

Distinct from Competitor Profile: that grades how well each alternative serves the people the offering is for; this draws lessons from how others solved similar problems, whether or not they compete. Absence invites reinvention.

sections.name: Prior art
sections.question: How have others solved problems like ours?

guidance.claim: Three lists, not two: included, deferred with a revisit trigger, and excluded with the reason.
Distinct from Trade-offs: scope excludes parts of the solution for this work; Trade-offs refuses directions for the offering as a whole.
The excluded list is the valuable one — it prevents silent re-expansion.
The deferred list is where natural extensions land — the RFC tradition's future possibilities.

sections.name: Scope in out
sections.question: What do we include in the solution now, defer, or exclude?

guidance.claim: 'Improve X' invites post-hoc rationalisation. Set a threshold and a measurement date.
Per-initiative acceptance, set before the work, expiring with the effort — unlike metrics that run continuously.
A product requirements document's launch 'success metrics' and an OKR's key results belong here: each is a threshold with a date, usually on an input metric.
Point to the shared measures the work must not break instead of copying them, and state in full each threshold this work commits to.

sections.name: Success criteria
sections.question: What observable result counts as success for the work?

guidance.claim: A user story (as-a / I-want / so-that) presumes a persona; a job story (when / I-want / so-I-can) presumes a circumstance. Pick one per document; do not mix.
Acceptance criteria turn a story from a conversation-starter into testable scope.
Distinct from Jobs to Be Done: ask whether the line names what the solution must let a person do. A story does, and acceptance criteria test it; the job behind it stays true whatever is built.

sections.name: User job stories
sections.question: What should the solution let a person do?

guidance.claim: Distinct from User / Job Stories: a story says what the solution should let a person do, one capability at a time; a trace follows one person through the solution in one circumstance, step by step, joins included.
The joins are the content. No single story contains a seam, and a set of stories does not sum to one trace.

Distinct from Solution Overview: a trace follows one person in one concrete circumstance in full detail; the overview outlines all the behaviour at once. Ask whether the text follows one path or covers them all. In a design document, refer to the trace where the RFC template puts its guide-level explanation.

sections.name: Stepwise trace
sections.question: What happens at each step of one path through the solution?

guidance.claim: Give each category its identifier and the fields its entries carry, so the model fixes the shape of an entry and not only its name.
Use each category's name the same way everywhere: in conversation, in documents and in the system itself. Keep it stable once other parts depend on it.
Record the categories and their fields, with only as many example entries as a reader needs to understand them. A full list of entries is the offering's data and belongs with it.
Documents that use these categories refer to this model for them, so each category is defined in one place.

sections.name: Canonical model
sections.question: Which named categories does the system use?

guidance.claim: Record each finding with how precisely it was measured and when it was observed. An undated survey cannot say whether it still holds.

Distinct from Constraints: the survey records what is actually in place; a constraint is a limit imposed on the work. A measured clearance is a finding here; a rule forbidding building into it is a constraint.

sections.name: As built survey
sections.question: What do measurements of the existing state show?

sections.name: Consent and authority
sections.question: What licence, permit, consent or legal basis allows the work?
